sections.heading: Naming what is wrong in my ministry
sections.text:
Blessed Spirit of God, I need to be honest with you about the sins and weaknesses that keep showing up in my work.

The enemy presses me down with discouragement and shame, especially when my own private time with you has been cold and thin. I can become careless, sluggish, and foggy in spirit. Sometimes past usefulness or other people’s approval makes me act as if present unfaithfulness does not matter.

I feel my weakness. I lack spiritual light, life, and power. People have not been helped as they should have been, and I have not felt your nearness. And sometimes, even when I have tried my best, there has still been little visible fruit.
theological_themes: honest confession of ministerial weakness
discouragement and spiritual attack
spiritual dryness in private devotion
the danger of pride after past usefulness
dependence on the Holy Spirit for fruitful ministry

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes ministry as received by God’s mercy and carried in fragile servants, so the power is clearly God’s and not the minister’s. This grounds the prayer’s honesty about weakness without giving up the calling.

Paul teaches that Christian service takes place amid real spiritual opposition. This supports naming discouragement as something the enemy can use, while still seeking strength from God rather than collapsing under shame.

sections.heading: Remembering where any usefulness comes from
sections.text:
You have been teaching me that nothing I do has glory in itself. If my preaching, counsel, study, or service is ever made useful, it is because you have set it apart and breathed life into it.

The gift is not the source. The servant is not the Savior. Any good that comes through me comes from you.
theological_themes: God as the source of all spiritual fruit
ministry made useful by divine grace
humility about gifts and results

scripture_references.connection: Paul distinguishes human labor from God’s life-giving work: one plants and another waters, but God gives the growth. This directly supports the prayer’s claim that usefulness in ministry comes from God, not from the worker.
Jesus teaches that his disciples can bear fruit only by abiding in him. This grounds the prayer’s refusal to treat ministry skill or effort as self-sufficient.

sections.heading: Centering my work on Christ
sections.text:
So bring me back to the true purpose of my ministry: to know Christ and to make his truth known.

Let Christ himself be the ground I stand on, the One I trust, and the strength I draw from. All fullness, life, and power are in him. Let my comfort in the work be this: that I am doing it for him, not for my reputation, my security, or my need to be seen as successful.
theological_themes: Christ as the center of ministry
preaching Christ rather than self
trusting Christ’s sufficiency
serving for Christ’s glory instead of reputation

scripture_references.connection: Paul deliberately centers his ministry on Christ crucified rather than impressive speech or human wisdom, so faith rests on God’s power. This supports the prayer’s desire to know Christ and impart his truth without depending on personal impressiveness.
Paul describes proclaiming Christ and laboring with Christ’s energy working in him. This fits the prayer’s movement from ministerial effort to dependence on Christ’s own strength.

sections.heading: Asking to be made humble through everything
sections.text:
Help me, in the middle of this work, to become more humble. In every circumstance you send or allow, teach me something that brings me lower before you and nearer to you.

Teach me to rejoice in you and to hate the pride, self-trust, and sin that still cling to me. Keep my life, my body, my soul, my time, and my calling for you alone. Let me not treat any part of myself as my own private possession.
theological_themes: humility through providence
repentance from pride and self-reliance
whole-person surrender to God
joy in God over self-importance

scripture_references.connection: James calls believers to humility before God, resistance to pride, and deep repentance. This supports the prayer’s request to be brought low in a way that leads to grace rather than despair.
Paul urges believers to offer their bodies to God as a living sacrifice in view of his mercy. This grounds the prayer’s desire that life, body, soul, and calling belong wholly to God.
Paul teaches that God works all things for the good of conforming his people to Christ. This supports asking God to use every providence, even humbling ones, for deeper holiness.

sections.heading: Wanting you more than visible success
sections.text:
Draw my heart to you with real love and delight. Help me see that every grace in me is yours, comes from you, and leads me back to you. Let me walk with you closely and tenderly, not merely work for you at a distance.

Then, whether my ministry seems to succeed or fail, let this be enough for me: you are mine, and I am yours. More than results, approval, usefulness, or comfort, I want you yourself.
theological_themes: communion with God above ministry outcomes
assurance rooted in belonging to God
contentment in God rather than visible fruit
grace received from and returned to God

scripture_references.connection: Paul’s central concern is that Christ be honored in him, whether through life or death, because Christ himself is his life. This supports the prayer’s longing for God to matter more than visible outcomes.
The psalmist confesses that God himself is his deepest desire and lasting portion. This illuminates the prayer’s final movement: success and failure are not ultimate when God himself is treasured.
Paul says the believer’s aim is to please the Lord. This supports the prayer’s desire to measure ministry by faithfulness to God rather than by reputation or visible success alone.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original attributes discouragement and shame to the devil. The adaptation preserves the reality of spiritual opposition without implying that every experience of discouragement is directly demonic or that ordinary human weakness, fatigue, or sin are irrelevant.

The phrase “loathe myself” is spiritually intense and can be misunderstood today as contempt for one’s personhood. I rendered it as hatred of pride, self-trust, and sin, preserving the Puritan concern for repentance without suggesting hatred of God’s image-bearing creature or denial of grace.
The original speaks of ministry success and failure. The adaptation keeps the concern for real usefulness while avoiding a simplistic equation of faithfulness with visible or measurable results.

Directly addressing the Holy Spirit is consistent with Trinitarian Christian prayer, though some traditions more commonly address the Father through the Son by the Spirit. The adaptation retains the original address to the Spirit.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Natural dullness and dimness of spirit” was rendered as being sluggish and foggy in spirit, not as an excuse rooted in personality but as a weakness needing God’s help.

“The glory of everything that is sanctified to do good is not seen in itself, but in the source of its sanctification” was interpreted to mean that gifts, sermons, and ministry acts are useful only because God makes them so.
“Souls have not been helped” was expressed as people not being helped as they should have been, preserving the pastoral burden while using more natural contemporary language.
“Whether I succeed or fail, nought matters but thee alone” was rendered as God being desired above results, approval, usefulness, and comfort—not as indifference to the spiritual good of others.
